item.title: Healing Means Coming Home to Oneself
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

Healing Means Coming Home to Oneself

Personal Perspective: What brought me home was a mother who kept showing up.

Posted September 9, 2026

Key points
  • Medication can steady the brain’s circuits, but the soul heals between people, not inside a single patient.
  • Attunement—a caregiver mirroring inner states—is not limited to infancy. It is recovery’s foundation.
  • Not every family member can make the journey. Some reach the empathy ceiling, which is not always cruelty.
  • My mother kept the light on in a room I was not yet ready to enter. Her witness made recovery possible.
Source: Justyna Sieczka/Pexels

The first afternoon of my release from a mental health facility, my mother pressed the keys to a car she had bought me into my hand. It was not a ceremony, and there was no speech. She handed them over, as though the act were ordinary—though nothing about it was.

I had spent 10 months inside a Wisconsin forensic psychiatric hospital after accepting a not-guilty-by-reason-of-mental-disease plea on eight felony charges arising from a psychotic manic episode. Lithium had brought order after a decade of neural dysregulation. The institution had provided structure, medication, and enforced stillness behind two barbed-wire fences, in which something resembling insight could solidify into meaning. But the hospital had not healed me. It had stabilized me, which is a different endeavor entirely, the way that stopping a hemorrhage is different from restoring the blood.

What the hospital could not offer was what I needed most: a relationship in which I could be seen again.

My mother, Linda, became the bridge back.

This was by no means foreordained. For years during my untreated illness, I had sent her messages of breathtaking cruelty—called her my Judas, disparaged her character, and weaponized her vulnerabilities with the fluency of a man whose intellect had been conscripted by mania. Anosognosia—the neurological inability to recognize one’s own illness—had made me experience her concern as a kind of persecution. I had pushed her away with a force that, for many other mothers, would have been permanent.

Every message landed. She stayed anyway, making a decision that was daily and costly and unromantic to keep witnessing a son whose illness had made him unrecognizable, on the faith that the person she remembered was still somewhere inside.

During my months at the hospital, she visited regularly. We read Kay Redfield Jamison’s An Unquiet Mind together and discussed its meaning to our lives over the ward phone. We learned about bipolar disorder side by side, not as teacher and student but as two people assembling a shared language for something that had nearly destroyed them both. What we built was more tentative but more honest than anything our prior relationship had contained. And when I walked out of the hospital, she was there with the car keys, not because everything was resolved—but because the process of meaningful repair had begun, and ongoing repair requires continued presence.

article continues after advertisement

What I have come to understand is that recovery is not a hermetic project of one. Medication can calm the brain's electrical chaos. Therapy can reorganize the mind's predictive patterns. But the soul, the part of us that knows itself through our relation to others, heals in the space between people. Recovery, at its most essential, is relational.

Source: Etienne Boulanger/Unsplash

Developmental psychologist Daniel Stern noted that even before language, infants and caregivers communicate through what he called vitality affects—mutual rhythms of feeling, moments when the caregiver mirrors the child’s inner state in a different sensory register. Susan Vaughn, in The Talking Cure, observes how these exchanges occur roughly once every two minutes in healthy pairs, the mother reflecting to the child an understanding of his current way of being. When asked why they responded as they did, mothers often said they were trying to “share the infant’s experience.” In these moments, Stern suggested, is nothing less than the “shape of and extent of the shareable inner universe.”

This magnificent exchange is called attunement, and it does not end in infancy. As Daniel Goleman writes in Emotional Intelligence, several psychoanalytic theories see therapy itself as a “reparative experience of attunement,” in which the therapist mirrors the client’s inner state “just as an attuned mother does with her infant.” The neuroscientist Stephen Porges, as Gabor and Daniel Maté note in The Myth of Normal, identifies reciprocity and attunement as among our most fundamental needs: to be, in the archaic greeting of the medieval world, “well met.”

In a previous column, I described how my therapist Susan became the first person after my release who truly saw me, not as a risk score or a clinical profile but as a whole person. What my mother was doing, across the longer trajectory of our reconciliation, was the same work in a different key. She was attuning to me—not perfectly, not without friction—but with the persistent attention that only someone who has known you for decades can provide. Thomas Lewis, Fari Amini, and Richard Lannon, in A General Theory of Love, call this knowing the deepest labor of love: “the prolonged and detailed surveillance of a foreign soul.” If that does not describe a mother’s attunement to a son she has watched for over 40 years, through the illness and the slow return, I do not know what does.

article continues after advertisement

But not everyone in a family can make this journey. Recovery asks something colossal of the people surrounding the person who has been at once ill and savage: it asks them to hold, simultaneously, the person who caused real harm and the person now recovering in the room in the same frame. Some family members jump in. Others reach what I have called the empathy ceiling: a limit beyond which understanding becomes too costly, too uncertain, too destabilizing to the comforting story they have constructed for themselves about what happened. I have come to believe this is not mercilessness but self-preservation. But it means the person recovering must learn to accept a profound asymmetry: that not every relationship will be repaired on the same timeline, or at all.

My mother jumped in. She made that choice—daily, actively, and at great personal cost. And what I want to name as forthrightly as I can is that her choice was not incidental to my recovery. It was intrinsic to it. Without her attunement—without our morning calls, the cribbage games at the kitchen table, the willingness to read my memoir and let it change what she understood, and to share her own journal and let it change what I understood—the medication would have still helped to manage my symptoms. But it would not have restored my life.

Recovery, at its deepest, is the work of becoming known again by someone patient enough to look past what the illness did and remember who you were before it spoke in your voice. It is coming home to yourself through the presence of someone who kept the light on in a room you were not yet ready to enter.

My mother kept the light on. And when I finally walked back through the door, she was still there.

item.title: A Simple Way to Get Over Disappointment Faster
item.description:
Emotion Regulation

A Simple Way to Get Over Disappointment Faster

The “Memoir Test” can help you stop small letdowns from taking over your mood.

Posted September 9, 2026

Key points
  • Disappointment is often painful because reality did not meet our expectations.
  • Feeling disappointed is valid, but giving the feeling a time limit can keep it from turning into rumination.
  • The “Memoir Test” can help you decide whether a disappointment deserves more of your emotional energy.

Disappointment is one of the most common, painful emotions we experience. It shows up when something we hoped for or expected does not happen. Your favorite team loses. You get sick before a trip. A friend cancels plans you were looking forward to. A job opportunity falls through. A dinner, date, or vacation does not go the way you imagined.

Disappointment can bring up many other feelings: frustration, regret, embarrassment, anger, resentment, hopelessness, or sadness. And while those feelings are understandable, the problem is that sometimes we stay in them for too long. A letdown that should sting for a few hours can turn into a bad mood that lasts for days. We replay what happened, think about what could have been, feel like victims, and wonder why things never go our way.

Here is a simple strategy I use with my clients, and in my own life, to recover from disappointment more quickly. It has two steps.

1. Feel the Disappointment, but Give It a Time Limit

When something disappointing happens, the goal is not to pretend you’re fine. Disappointment is your mind’s way of recognizing that you lost something you wanted, expected, or hoped for. You’re allowed to feel upset. In fact, it’s important to acknowledge your feelings. But validating your feelings does not mean letting them take over.

To avoid getting stuck, consider the size and meaning of the disappointment. How important was it? How much will it matter later? How does it compare to other disappointments you have dealt with? Then give yourself a reasonable amount of time to feel bad about it.

If your favorite team lost a regular game, maybe you give yourself an hour. If they lost the championship, maybe you give yourself a day. If a dinner plan fell through, maybe you feel annoyed that evening, but you do not let it ruin the whole weekend.

The point is not to rush yourself through your feelings. The point is to give them boundaries. Without boundaries, disappointment can easily become a loop of “what could have been” and “what should have happened,” and that loop is where we tend to get stuck.

2. Use the Memoir Test

Once your “feeling bad time” is up, use this thought exercise to shift your perspective: Imagine you’re writing a memoir about your life 20 or 30 years from now. Would this disappointment make it into the book? Most disappointments would not. You probably would not devote pages of your life story to the dinner that went badly, the client who never called back, the rainy weekend, the missed party, or the plan that fell apart. Not because those moments did not hurt—they did—but in the larger story of your life, they’re not that important.

article continues after advertisement

That is the Memoir Test. You ask yourself: Will this matter enough to make it into the story of my life? To answer the question, use mental time travel. Project yourself forward to that future version of you, looking back. From that vantage point, many years from now, will you still be upset about this? Will you even remember it clearly? Will it have changed the direction of your life? Often, the answer will be no, and realizing that can make it easier to let go.

Most disappointments are footnotes in our life story, not major plot twists. They hurt in the moment, but they rarely define us unless we keep giving them that power. So the next time you feel the sting of disappointment, acknowledge it, give yourself some time to feel bad, then run the Memoir Test and put the incident into perspective.

Adapted from my newsletter, The Psychology Lab.

item.title: Can AI Have Conscious Experiences?
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Can AI Have Conscious Experiences?

The answer to the question of AI consciousness is no.

Posted September 9, 2026

Key points
  • Did you know that AI has been around since 1956 as a subarea within cognitive science.
  • Did you know that consciousness was somewhat taboo in early cognitive science, including AI.
  • Did you know that human consciousness is the product of hundreds of millions of years of animal evolution?
  • How could we tell if AI is conscious given it is so hard to demonstrate consciousness in non-human animals?

The Birth of AI

AI is the hottest game in town. But you may be surprised to know that it is not a new-fangled thing. It emerged decades ago, in 1956 to be exact.

I first came across AI when writing my 1996 book, The Emotional Brain. As the title implies, the book was about emotion; at the time, emotion was second fiddle to cognition. Because of this, I titled chapter two “Souls on Ice,” about passion versus reason, feeling versus thinking, emotion versus cognition.

Much of the chapter focused on the origin of cognitive science, especially cognitive psychology, in the late 1940s and early 1950s. To break with behaviorism, cognitive psychologists sought to bring the mind back into psychology. But they did not bring back the conscious mind that John Watson and his behaviorist followers had banned from psychology in the early 20th century. Instead, they treated the mind as an information processing system.

Whether a cognitive scientist was a psychologist, computer engineer, or philosopher, or some other kind of researcher, they tended to be pro-cognition and anti-consciousness at the time. As a result, computer operations became metaphors for human cognition (language, logic, rationality), and computer simulations came to be used to understand human cognition. Indeed, in the early years, AI’s programmers sought to achieve human-like intelligence (cognition) in machines to help solve scientific problems, which it did. Current AI programming ambitions go much further, with some claiming that AI has, or will have, human-like consciousness. That’s quite a change from the early anti-consciousness days of cognitive science.

Cognition in Neuroscience

Much of the contemporary discussion of AI and consciousness is about the brain. Before further discussion, we need to see how neuroscience fits into this picture. Neuroscience emerged in the late 1960s, roughly two decades after cognitive science. I worked on my Ph.D. on consciousness and the human brain in the 1970s. AI was about 20 years old then, and I didn’t think about it much because I was far more interested in why consciousness was taboo within certain circles in neuroscience. I discovered why from personal experience.

After obtaining my Ph.D., I turned to studies of the brain mechanisms of emotional behavior in rats and submitted my first grant proposal to NIMH in 1984. I had no illusion about studying emotional consciousness in animals, as my goal was to study emotional behavior. But the grant was rejected because "neuroscientists do not study emotion.” The reviewers were very likely either cognitive psychologists or lingering behaviorists. In either case, they opposed subjective experience being studied in neuroscience and viewed the word “emotion” as a kind of “consciousness,” which was not what the grant was about.

article continues after advertisement

I carefully revised the proposal by focusing on the method I used, Pavlovian conditioning of behavior, and received five years of funding, followed by 25 years of support. I published the empirical work on rats in neuroscience journals, and I also wrote about human consciousness in my books: The Emotional Brain (1996), Synaptic Self 2002), Anxious (2015), The Deep History of Ourselves (2019), and The Four Realms of Existence (2023).

I am now retired and continue to write about consciousness, which can be why I receive requests to comment about “AI and Consciousness?” Personally, I do not believe that AI can be conscious, and below I explain why.

The Deep History of Our Four Realms of Existence

In The Four Realms of Existence, I defined the realms in terms of evolutionary transitions over the roughly four-billion-year history of life on Earth. Specifically, the four realms are biological, neurobiological, cognitive, and conscious ways of existing. All living organisms exist biologically. Some biological organisms, namely animals, evolved nervous systems, which allowed more complex control of biological survival functions by using automatic stimulus-response reflexes and habits in ways that mere biological organisms lacked. Some neurobiological organisms went on to evolve cognitive capacities, which make possible the use of internal representations of the inner and outer worlds when evaluating outcomes and choosing what to do. Finally, some cognitive creatures evolved the ability to be consciously aware of their internal representations and can tell others about their inner thoughts and feelings. The bottom line is that while human consciousness (that is, subjective experience) depends on cognition, having cognition does not, by itself, endow humans or any other animals with human-like consciousness.

I am not saying that other animals do not have their own kind of consciousness based on their own kind of cognition. They may, but the evidence is mostly speculative, something I have written about extensively. But the issue here is about AI, not animal consciousness. That said, if we can’t definitively tell from behavioral outputs whether a non-human animal is responding consciously or unconsciously, and we certainly can’t, how could we possibly use the output of a machine to tell us it is conscious?

article continues after advertisement

Why AI Can't Have Human Consciousness

Let’s start with the belief that consciousness is just something that neural cir­cuits do in humans. If so, it would seem that making computers “self-­ aware conscious agents” would be a ­matter of figuring out the circuitry in detail, duplicating its connectivity digitally, and querying the resulting machine about its conscious states. But I don’t think that does the trick.

In The Deep History of Ourselves I told the four-billion-year story of how we got conscious brains, starting with the first biological organisms (single-cell bacteria-like organisms) and going all the way to present-day humans. A crucial transition was the evolution of organisms with nervous systems; that is, animals. Then it took hundreds of millions of years for animals to evolve ner­vous systems with the kind of cir­cuits we have. But creating conscious machines is not just about creating human-like brain circuits. Knowing the cir­cuit particulars is essential for understanding how our brains make us conscious. But that is not sufficient to understand human consciousness, much less be the basis for reflective “self-awareness” in a non-­biological physical system.

Particularly important is the fact that brain circuits are not just neural wires. They depend on microscopic cellular, molecular, and ge­ne­tic adaptations that preceded nervous systems by billions of years. Solving how these adaptations in AI would not be a matter of identifying and re­-creating each microscopic change; the changes would have to take place within a perfect re-creation of the environments in which the changes occurred and persisted over time. Moreover, it would be necessary to factor in the impact of feedback to the nervous system from behavioral activities that evolved in response to ­dynamic environmental conditions at each step along the way.

Even if all that was possible, the question that would remain unanswerable is whether there is any "there there." In other words, would a perfect computer simulation that accounts for all the factors above actually have conscious states of the kind that developed through biological, neurobiological, cognitive, and conscious evolution, or would it just be capable of generating a sophisticated set of responses that resemble ­those of humans? I go for the latter.

My bottom-line conclusion can be summarized as a chain of incorrectness. Specifically, the idea of conscious AI confuses physicality with biology -> biology with neurobiology -> neurobiology with cognition -> and cognition with consciousness.

item.title: Why "Mind Reading" Is Coming for Psychedelic Neuroscience
item.description:
Mind Reading

Why "Mind Reading" Is Coming for Psychedelic Neuroscience

Neuroscientists are decoding brain activity to uncover the nature of mind.

Posted September 9, 2026

Mind reading is no longer science fiction.

In 2006, in the journal Science, neuroscientists unequivocally showed that hospitalized, unresponsive patients can actually communicate with the outside world through their brain activity alone. Ask a "yes" or "no" question, and receive an answer based on what the patient is visualizing or imagining inside: playing tennis for "yes," or walking through their home for "no," each inner experience yielding markedly distinct patterns of brain activity.

More recently, with the introduction of machine learning and artificial intelligence, neuroscientists working with healthy participants have been able to decode and reconstruct various presented stimuli, from individual letters to entire scenes, capturing what the mind sees on screen. The same researchers who published the landmark study in 2006 are now asking how these reconstructions may be applied to similar patient populations to unlock a clearer window into their mind, and with it, greater communication with the outside world.

In 1968, Alan Watts lays the foundation for psychedelic science with his article Psychedelics and Religious Experience. There, he characterizes psychedelics as "instruments for studying and describing that experience as one uses a microscope for bacteriology." However, nearly 60 years later, Watts' intuition that psychedelics are observational instruments has gained little momentum, at least outside of their emerging application in clinical settings for occasioning personal psychological insights and emotional breakthroughs that predict improvements in mental health and well-being. Where are the data on the general nature of experience, of the mind, of consciousness itself? If a psychedelic can serve as an observational instrument, where is the evidence?

Returning to Watt's analogy to microscopic phenomena, let's consider Rosalind Franklin's discovery of the structure of DNA. Franklin's major discovery, her evidence, did not rest on her ability to see beyond, to peer through a microscope, but rather to capture what was there, right inside of what we know now as Photo 51. She and her graduate student took this photograph of DNA fibers, ultimately revealing DNA's structure to the world. This is exactly what is missing in psychedelic neuroscience and why mind reading is coming for the field: to reconstruct the same observations that were once apparent to Watts, only now validated across participants in the world's first-of-their-kind empirical studies of mind. Whereas Franklin's discovery unlocked the blueprint of life, giving rise to modern molecular biology and genetic medicine, what might the blueprint of mind lie ahead for our future?

Photo 51 (in pink)
Source: Conor Murray

item.title: Near-Death Experiences and the Grief No One Names
item.description:
Near-Death Experiences

Near-Death Experiences and the Grief No One Names

Why coming back changed from a NDE can mean losing a shared reality.

Posted September 9, 2026

Key points
  • Near-death experiences are far from rare.
  • The aftermath of an NDE often includes an unnamed grief: the loss of a shared reality.
  • NDE experiencers can benefit from relational curiosity and people who can tolerate not-knowing.
Source: Jeremy Thomas / Unsplash

A client who survived a near-death experience (NDE) came back with a word for everyone else: “muggles,” borrowed from Harry Potter, where it names people born without magic. She meant it affectionately, having learned that describing what happened to her exceeded what most people could psychologically receive.

My client wasn’t being unkind when she called folks “muggles.” Most people, in her experience, were living ordinary lives with little room for what she’d been through. After all, she essentially experienced firsthand a mythic unraveling and psycho-spiritual reconstruction in the face of existential annihilation. I think it’s fair to say this isn’t your average Tuesday. So, the beauty and terror of her near-death experience exceeded what most people in her life could take in, so they became “muggles,” unaware that another world had opened alongside the ordinary one they shared with her.

Near-Death Experiences

According to a scoping review, as many as one in three cardiac arrest survivors may have a near-death experience (NDE), which in a nutshell is an altered state of consciousness that can occur when a person is physiologically and psychologically close to death.1 The research evidence makes it clear these are not fringe events that happen to only a select few, and NDEs aren’t limited to cardiac arrest; NDE’s can occur in any circumstance where a person comes close to death. Scientists have not yet determined why some people have an NDE in these situations, and others don’t.

In my own clinical work, people have often described these experiences as “realer than real,” which is also what researchers have found when interviewing people who consciously remember their near-death experiences.

Source: Baatcheet Films / Unsplash

Research captures how these individuals are often permanently changed by the experience.2 Frequently, individuals report an out-of-body experience, emotions associated with transcendence, the experience of heading to a destination, meaningful interactions with deceased relatives or spiritual figures, awareness of death itself, and a sense of returning to life and awakening from this experience with a mystical appreciation of the nature of their life or the universe itself. The literature also captures how most people who experience a NDE have an intense desire to share about their experience, and yet frequently find it challenging to open up due to fear of rejection, minimization, bullying, or being pathologized by medical or healthcare professionals.

One study found that roughly one in five disclosures left the NDE survivor feeling harmed by the professional they told, across every professional group studied. What was more troubling was that the people with the deepest, most intense NDEs, the ones who arguably needed support the most, were the ones most likely to have their disclosure dismissed or treated as a sign of something wrong with them.3

While NDEs can be deeply enriching and psycho-spiritually transformative, these mystical experiences can be accompanied by a distinct kind of relational grief.

Loss of a Shared Reality

After an NDE, a person often comes back changed, sometimes radically so, and discovers that the shared reality they used to take for granted—the assumption that other people basically live in the same world they do—has quietly come apart. This loss of the assumptive world is what my client was grieving: not the NDE itself, but the relational distance it opened between her and everyone who hadn’t had one, or for other people who simply were not psycho-spiritually curious.

That grief resurfaced every time she met someone new, or talked to someone she’d known for years who wasn’t open to hearing about the experience. She grappled with another moment of having to decide whether this person could hold what she was carrying, or whether she’d need to offer a smaller, safer, non-transcendent and inauthentic version of her story instead.

Grief researchers call this kind of ongoing, non-death-related loss a nonfinite loss: a loss with no clear endpoint and no concrete ritual to mark it, since nothing has died in the conventional sense.4 It also overlaps with the clinical concept of chronic sorrow, since the grief experience involves persistent emotional reactions to ongoing relational adjustment; in essence, the person must keep continuously readjusting to their relational, familial, and communal situation.5

It’s a unique form of distress precisely because there’s no foreseeable end to it. Most readers can likely appreciate how exhausting and relationally grueling it is to keep entering a state of uncertainty, never knowing whether the next person you tell will react with curiosity or judgment to your most intimate and vulnerable story. For my client, that uncertainty opened a painful gap between the reality of how people responded and what she continued to hope for, which was to simply be understood (w)holistically.

Tolerating Not-Knowing

It makes sense that NDEs stir up so much in the people who hear about them, as they brush up against the big philosophical questions most of us never fully resolve: What’s real, what happens when we die, and is there more to this life than what we can see or measure? So, in response, many people engage in defensive black-and-white thinking where they want to file the story away as either true or false, insane or sane, etc., so that the existential tension of the messy questions can stop pressing against themselves.

My invitation to readers is this: Can you tolerate not knowing? Can you enter a curious, empathetic, relationally other-oriented stance long enough to let someone tell you the truth of what they carry, whether you can fully comprehend it or not?

That psychological tolerance and sense of curiosity, rather than a particular belief, is often what determines whether the people we care about feel like they’re returning to a shared world after an NDE or quietly building a new life in a world we’ll never be let into.

item.title: What Happiness Frameworks Keep Getting Wrong
item.description:
Happiness

What Happiness Frameworks Keep Getting Wrong

Edward Perper spent 18 years reading the research on happiness, and kept finding the same gap.

Posted September 9, 2026

Key points
  • Our memory of experiences is shaped more by how they end than by how long they last.
  • Most happiness frameworks explain the past but don’t map the future clearly.
  • The "four pairs" approach examines where a present choice is likely to lead.
Most of us are following the arrow. Fewer of us are asking where it leads.
Source: D Jonez / Unsplash

In the 1990s, the Nobel laureate Daniel Kahneman ran a study on colonoscopy patients. Some had the instrument withdrawn quickly at the end of the procedure, producing a sharp final moment of discomfort. Others had it withdrawn more slowly, extending the procedure but ending on a milder sensation. The latter group rated the overall experience as less unpleasant: They had more total discomfort, and they remembered it better.

This is the peak-end rule: We don’t evaluate experiences by averaging how they felt moment to moment. We judge them by their most intense moment and by how they ended. The duration largely vanishes from our evaluation.

For Edward Perper, a cardiologist who spent 18 years reading more than 1,000 research papers on well-being, the finding raised a more uncomfortable question: If memory of experience is this systematically distorted, what exactly are we optimizing for when we pursue happiness?

Perper explored answers from several traditions, including Freudian therapy, Jungian analysis, Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT), Buddhism and Stoicism. He saw value in each, but argues that they answer different questions: Freudian approaches ask why you do what you do. CBT focuses on changing the thinking patterns that drive behaviour. Buddhism encourages detachment from outcomes. Stoicism recommends you accept what you cannot control.

Perper believes we're still missing a forward-looking tool: a way to ask, in the moment, if something we're doing is likely to make us happier later, or more miserable, or simply: Will this lead to more happiness or more unhappiness?

This the gap that what Perper calls The Four Pairs of Happiness are designed to fill.

The Four Pairs

The framework is simple: Any activity, Perper suggests, can be mapped by two variables: how it feels now, and how it is likely to feel later.

Two possible feelings now (happy or unhappy), times the same two possible feelings later (happy or unhappy) produces four combinations.

  • Gold: Happy now, happy later. These are enjoyable activities that produce even more joy.

  • Grit: Unhappy now, happy later. These are difficult things tat are still worth doing, like exercise, learning, or having difficult conversations.

  • Trap: Happy now, unhappy later. Addiction is the clearest example of this, but it could also be the sugary snack that mitigates hunger but becomes a habit or the pleasant distraction that compounds into avoidance.

  • Crash: Unhappy now, unhappy later. These represent the patterns we maintain despite knowing that they lead nowhere better.

Perper's framework isn’t intended to diagnose or treat. Its purpose is simply to give people names for patterns that may be invisible to them but that, with intentional effort, can become recognizable. And he has found that this naming is often what people are missing: a way to see the structure of their own patterns.

When Perper first mapped the four pairs, he assumed certain combinations would dominate. Grit, he expected, would be most commonly missed—people not recognising that discomfort now might mean happiness later. He was right about that. What surprised him more was how common Gold turned out to be.

“People find a way to make those H-H moments happen,” he told me. Often these are small, unremarkable moments, like a quiet cup of coffee, a conversation that goes somewhere unexpected, a completed task the delivers more satisfaction than expected. Thus, the idea Perper most wants to challenge, he told me, is that happiness only counts in its most extreme forms. These moments are everywhere, he believes; we're just not labeling them.

There is also, he explains, a nesting phenomenon. A Grit pair, for example, can sit inside a Gold one. Building something sustainable can require an unpleasant period of discipline. Over time, that Grit can become part of a self-sustaining Gold pattern.

The Cardiologist Who Left

Perper was a practicing cardiologist, and his profession suited him in some ways but not in others. The stress, the difficult conversations, the weight of the work—in retrospect, he realizes, he had been in what he would now call a Trap: pleasant enough in its rewards, but leading somewhere he didn’t want to go. And so, he left. He found medical education and science visualisation, work that engaged him differently. He describes the transition as a recognition: He had finally seen the pair he was in clearly enough to step out of it.

Perper's four pairs, he insists, is not a theory of happiness but a vocabulary for noticing already-exisiting patterns.

Kahneman’s colonoscopy patients forgot how long it hurt but remembered how it ended. Which parts of your own experiences are shaping the way you remember them—and which do you barely notice at all?

item.title: Why It's So Hard to Change
item.description:
Habit Formation

Why It's So Hard to Change

Henrik Ibsen's character Nora was courageous.

Posted September 9, 2026

Key points
  • Our brains perceive uncertainty as a threat.
  • Change rarely feels good in the moment, and maintaining the status quo feels safe.

In Henrik Ibsen’s play A Doll’s House, Nora wakes to the realization that she’s been living a false identity and chooses to leave it in the end, even at the enormous cost of leaving her children behind; a decision that remains shocking today. Contemporary criticism has reframed Nora’s exit as self-realization rather than abandonment. Her transformation is tied to autonomy and self-awareness. While extreme, her evolution is courageous and illustrates something universal: change, even when it’s necessary or good for us, rarely feels that way in the moment.

Our brains perceive uncertainty as a threat, which activates our fight-or-flight response. It’s as if our brains react to change, even when it's positive, as a trauma response, which may help explain why people who’ve lived through trauma sometimes find even positive change hard to tolerate. Maintaining the status quo feels safe, even when change could lead to recovery. We anchor ourselves to the status quo as a baseline for what feels normal. Once something becomes the default, it starts to feel like the correct state, and any deviation feels like it needs justification, even if the status quo itself was arbitrary.

What does the science say?

According to the transtheoretical model, change is a process with five stages:

  1. Precontemplation. An unconscious awareness that change is necessary. To move past this stage, we need to recognize that change is necessary.
  2. Contemplation. The stage where we make a plan for change by employing research as a necessary step to inform us about how to go about making changes
  3. Preparation. The stage where we start planning to change.
  4. Action. Executing our plan. To be successful, we develop strategies to stay on track.
  5. Maintenance. This stage typically occurs around the six-month mark, when the action we took begins to feel stable, less threatening, and more consistent.

While transtheoretical is a model, it’s often viewed as a spiral. Though the steps seem straightforward, we often regress to a previous stage. Not such a bad thing, since each time we start over, we get smarter and stronger.

Still, that doesn’t make change any easier. Behavioral economics calls this loss aversion. We feel the pain of losing something roughly twice as intensely as we feel the pleasure of an equivalent gain. Even a clearly “better” change registers emotionally as: What am I giving up?

Our identity gets tangled up in habits. The way we already do things becomes part of how we see ourselves. Changing behavior can feel like changing who we are, which is a much bigger ask than it looks on the surface.

Change also costs energy the brain would rather not spend. Established patterns run on autopilot. New ones require conscious effort. The effort feels like friction, which gives us reason to stop, stall, or freeze. This is especially pronounced when past change has gone badly. No one wants to make the same mistake twice. When earlier attempts to change something led to failure, humiliation, or harm, that history gets encoded, making the next attempt feel even riskier.

article continues after advertisement

Not so irrational, right? The problem isn’t that we resist change, but that we resist it reflexively, without weighing whether this particular change is worth the discomfort or effort to override the fight-or-flight response.

Let’s revisit Nora.

Early in the play, Nora appears as a woman shaped by years of trauma in a patriarchal environment. She is bubbly, childlike, and fawning. She lives only to appease her controlling husband. She masks her deep intelligence, financial stress, and the crime she committed to protect him behind the frivolous facade of a macaroon-eating shopaholic. She anticipates catastrophe and bases her sense of safety solely on her husband’s volatile approval. Yet in the end, she leaves behind the “dollhouse” and all its domestic trappings, including her children, choosing instead to live a life more in line with who she wants to be rather than the person she has become. That’s what makes her personality shift so abrupt and courageous.

Not everyone who has suffered trauma is poised to make life-altering decisions as Nora did. But her story offers something useful even in far smaller moments:

  • A habit we can’t seem to break.
  • A conversation we keep avoiding.
  • A version of ourselves we’ve outgrown but haven’t yet let go of because it might disappoint others.

Change will always feel like danger before it feels like relief. That’s not a character flaw. It’s how we’re built.

item.title: Supporting Your Parents Through Divorce as an Adult
item.description:
Divorce

Supporting Your Parents Through Divorce as an Adult

How to be there for your divorcing parents while protecting yourself.

Posted September 9, 2026

Key points
  • Listen to your parents with compassion, recognizing that you may not know all the details of their marriage.
  • Set boundaries around conversations and information that make you uncomfortable.
  • Support your parents without feeling obligated to approve of their choices or behavior.
Source: Matt Bennett / Unsplash

As an adult, watching your parents go through a divorce can be a disorienting experience. Your parents may have been your rock, your constants, the people you never thought would have wanted to go their separate ways after decades of marriage. Or you may have wondered for years why it took them so long to pull the plug.

Whatever the situation may be, it’s likely that your parents could use your support, emotional or otherwise, in beginning their next chapters. Even if you’re not thrilled about your parents’ splitting up or agree with their decision, there are ways you can be there for them.

Do Your Best to Understand Where They’re Coming From

You haven’t walked in your parents’ shoes. Nor have you been privy to what's been happening behind closed doors. This means that your parents each have a story to tell, and they may want to tell it to you.

Though it may not be a story you want to hear, try your hardest to demonstrate patience with them and listen until the point where it no longer feels comfortable for you, which, depending on how detailed they get, it may not.

Don’t Be Afraid to Establish Boundaries Around Off-Limits Topics

You may be an adult, but you’re still your parents’ child. Therefore, it’s natural for some subjects, such as your parents’ sex lives or other sensitive information, to cause you to feel uncomfortable or to feel that you’re learning of matters you believe should be kept private, or at least private from you.

If you ever feel this way, don’t be afraid to say so, and then set a firm boundary for which conversations are off limits and which are fair game.

Refrain From Judging Them (if You Can)

This is a big ask, especially if a parent confides in you something you find abhorrent, such as an affair, or some other form of deceit, like financial infidelity. You can voice your disapproval, but do your best not to chastise them, especially if they’re genuinely remorseful for past wrongs they cannot right.

article continues after advertisement

You don’t need to support these behaviors. But if you have it in you, put yourself in a place where you can be there for them today and as they move forward. If you cannot, be upfront about that, too.

Don’t Harbor Your Parents’ Secrets for Them

Set the record straight early on: You are not the keeper of your parents’ secrets, and you are not their confidant or therapist. Other people can fill these roles, including friends, family members who are not their children, and mental health professionals. You are there to support your parents as a child would — out of love and respect for them.

Don’t Be the Bearer of Bad News to Your Other Parent

If you do learn something from one parent that would be better off being communicated by that parent to your other parent, encourage them to do so directly. Unless one parent is in imminent danger from the other, give that parent a chance to say what they have to say to their ex-spouse first. The last thing you want is to become a go-between. Again, other people can carry this responsibility.

Show Your Support in a Way That’s Comfortable for You

It’s all right to show your solidarity with your divorcing parents in ways other than agreeing with them or listening to stories of past or current behavior you find distasteful. For instance, you can accompany them as they look for a new place to live, pack boxes, or help with other logistics, staying neutral as you help each begin building new lives apart.

article continues after advertisement

Everyone has limits, you included, and you should understand yours emotionally. Based on your availability, you can establish what you will and will not be able to do for your parents during this transitional time. Remember that "No" is an acceptable answer.

Remember That Their Divorce Is About Them, Not You

In the absence of an unusual circumstance, your parents’ divorce has everything to do with them and nothing to do with you. Every romantic relationship is unique. There are ebbs and flows, happy times and sad ones, and dynamics between individuals that can change as the years pass. You may have grown up in the same home as your parents, but the relationship you shared with them as a unit and as individuals was and is separate and apart from how they lived in that same home with each other.

A Last Word

Your parents’ divorce may hurt you for a while, or even forever, but what you will always share with them is a past. And now, as you develop a new understanding of your parents, not only as the individuals who raised you but as people with their own experiences, emotions, and reasons for the choices they have made, you may discover a different, perhaps deeper, way of relating to them and a meaningful next chapter in your family's story.

item.title: Parent Guilt: Finding a Part to Play Without Feeling Blamed
item.description:
Parenting

Parent Guilt: Finding a Part to Play Without Feeling Blamed

Medicalizing can relieve parent blame, but where does that leave parent agency?

Posted September 9, 2026

Key points
  • Medicalizing a child’s problem can relieve parent blame but may also reduce agency.
  • Parents can examine their part in patterns without taking blame for the whole problem.
  • A family systems lens helps parents become curious observers of their own reactivity.
  • Parent agency grows when guilt gives way to seeing what is within a parent’s control.

A mother recently wrote to me at The Parent Hope Project and asked:

“Would you be prepared to share your view on the parent guilt I’m struggling with?”

And in a recent client session, a dad said that the hardest thing for him in working on himself as a parent was managing his regrets and guilt.

It’s so very hard for parents not to feel burdened by guilt.

One understandable response has been to separate parents from their child’s problems. Medical explanations for children’s difficulties can provide relief by taking away the implication that parents caused the problem.

But a dilemma remains. If the problem is located entirely in a diagnosis, disorder, brain, gene, or other medical explanation, the parent may feel less blameworthy—but also less able to see where they can make a difference.

How do we separate a parent from blame without separating them from a meaningful part in their child’s recovery and well-being?

For me, this is where a family systems lens is so useful. It helps a parent avoid seeing the problem as all their fault while also recognizing that they have played a part in relationship patterns—and can play a part in changing them.

The key is shifting from guilt to becoming a curious observer—recognizing that there are things to discover within a parent’s control that can gradually make a difference.

As we put it in our Parent Hope manuals:

“Parents can play an important role in reducing symptoms by adjusting how they interact with their children. In this way, parents find that they can let go of guilt and recover their hopefulness.”

Parents do not need more guilt. But neither do they need to be positioned as having no part to play.

What parents themselves say

I have learned a lot from listening to parents’ experiences of guilt when one of their children is struggling with complex emotional and behavioral health issues.

In my qualitative research with parents who had an adolescent in a treatment program, I learned something important about leaving guilt behind while still looking at what parents can adjust.

Parents I interviewed at the end of their involvement in their child’s treatment spoke about realizing that their parenting had not always been helpful to their child’s well-being without taking on a sense of guilt.

The data revealed that blame was averted when the insights gained were useful and not imposed. When parents came to their own realization about the part they may unintentionally have played in their child’s ongoing symptoms—and could see what they might change—guilt could be laid aside and replaced with hopefulness.

One mother reflected:

“Just having that knowledge, I suppose, stops you feeling: ‘Gosh, I’ve been a bad parent’... You’ve just got caught up in something and not realizing you’re adding to it or making it harder to get out of… Having that knowledge… helps you to move on.”

“You’ve just got caught up in something” beautifully expresses a systems perspective.

The parent is neither the villain nor irrelevant to what is happening. They have become caught up in a relationship pattern. And because they are part of it, there are things they can do differently.

Another mother captured the shift from guilt to agency particularly clearly:

“It hasn’t given me any guilt or anything; it’s given me skills… I know I did the best I could.”

These parents were not being absolved of having any part in what was happening. Nor were they being blamed. They were being supported to think about themselves within a relationship system and find where they had room to move.

When guilt becomes agency

This growth in agency is an example of what family systems theory calls “working on differentiation of self.”

Differentiation is not about becoming detached from those we love. It is about learning to observe and manage our own reactivity, think more clearly when relationships become tense, and take responsibility for our own part rather than becoming absorbed in trying to change or blame another person.

For a parent, the question shifts from “How do I get my child to change?” to “What happens to me in this relationship, and what is mine to work on?”

This is very different from telling a parent, “You caused your child’s problem.” But it is also different from reassuring them, “This has nothing to do with you.” Neither position gives parents much useful room to move.

In my recent book The Parenting Paradox, I return to this dilemma. Parents want to do their best for their children’s well-being and are willing to consider their part in the development of problems if they believe they can make a positive difference.

Parents already hear plenty about what they should and shouldn’t be doing. Being told to stop being anxious can add to their guilt and leave them feeling patronized.

A systems perspective offers something different from both parent blame and parent absolution. It moves beyond linear cause-and-effect thinking towards seeing reciprocal patterns: how each person responds to the other and how these responses can intensify or settle a problem over time.

Parents need something more useful than either “This is your fault” or “There is nothing you can do.”

They need a pathway to agency.

From absolution to agency

Perhaps we need to ask a different question about parent guilt.

It is not simply: How do we reassure parents that they did not cause their child’s problems?

Parents certainly do not need to be blamed for the complex difficulties their children experience. But nor do they need to be positioned as helpless bystanders who must hand the problem entirely to professionals.

A more useful question is: How do we help parents become curious enough to see their part in a pattern without concluding that the whole problem is their fault?

This requires the kind of differentiation that allows a parent to stay lovingly connected to their child while becoming a more thoughtful observer of their own part in the relationship.

A parent can recognize:

I did not cause all of this.

I can observe my own reactivity rather than making myself or my child the problem.

What I do can make a difference.

This is not parental blame.

It is parental agency—and with agency comes hope.

item.title: Knowing What You Are Up Against in Your Own Self
item.description:
Addiction

Knowing What You Are Up Against in Your Own Self

We often lack perspective on ourselves.

Posted September 9, 2026

Key points
  • There are various forms of self-deception in addiction that can extend to recovery.
  • Perfectionism and procrastination are two unusual forms of self-deception.
  • In seeking self-knowledge, we may encounter distortions that are like fun house mirrors.
  • Self-knowledge is necessary for flourishing.

Active in our addictions, we are often susceptible to various forms of self-deception. There are the usual suspects that get trotted out regularly: denial, minimization, and rationalization. There are some unusual suspects that are often trickier to identify.

Perfectionism and Procrastination

One unusual suspect is perfectionism, which is the conviction and the actions that spring from that assumption that one should be able to do everything perfectly. Anything short of perfection is abject failure. A perfectionist fails to grasp what is in her control (intentions, attitudes, and efforts) by assuming she can control the outcomes or results of those actions.

Another unusual suspect is procrastination, which gets its power from the gap between wishing or wanting something and being willing to act in ways to make something more likely come to pass. Procrastination is putting something off that a person claims to want or need because their willingness is missing.

Our patterns may be so deeply engrained that we fail to see them. Many of us not yet in recovery or early in it believe that we must somehow be perfect in recovery, and the fear of not doing so keeps us from making a commitment to recovery sooner. We may tell ourselves that we will fully commit when everything in the universe is in alignment.

We fail to see that the universe may never align in the way we hope or expect.

The Difficulty of Self-knowledge

As we enter recovery, it's crucial to know what we’re up against in our own selves. As much as we might like to believe that in recovery we leave these forms of self-deception behind, we often don’t. We may get better at identifying and interrupting them earlier. Doing so is a matter of self-knowledge.

Self-knowledge can be incredibly difficult to achieve. Oftentimes we think that we are infallible when it comes to knowledge of ourselves. We take ourselves to have privileged access to the contents of our minds, and no one else can truly detect what we are thinking or feeling. If we have spent large periods of time wearing masks or presenting facades, this reinforces our view that we are infallible when it comes to our beliefs, motivations, efforts, feelings etc.

However, we may be hindered in seeing ourselves clearly or accurately because we lack perspective. We are too close to ourselves in some way. Think about the ways that as we age we may need to hold things further away so we can see them clearly. There really isn’t an equivalent when it comes to looking deep inside of ourselves.

article continues after advertisement

Our ability to see ourselves clearly, accurately, and charitably is also affected by reflections. Think of looking inside yourself as looking in a mirror. Mirrors always distort, even a flat or plane mirror. An image is always backward.

Our view of ourselves may be distorted by the curve of a mirror. Fun house mirrors distort; a concave mirror curves inward, making the image appear short and wide. A convex mirror curves outward, so the reflection is taller and thinner. Our most deeply held beliefs can be fun house mirrors. Consider that many of us in the worst throes of addiction become fixated on the belief that we are bad, incorrigible, irredeemable, and beyond any kind of measure.

One of the fun house beliefs that is especially pernicious is, I can never be sober. We may believe that we are incapable of doing so because we have failed so many times in the past. We may not be able to see that that fun house mirror belief along with the actions that spring from it is a type of self-deception.

Self-Examination in Service of Self-Knowledge

It's necessary that we loosen that fixation of beliefs, which is oftentimes accomplished only through a kind of intentional and rigorous self-examination. Philosophers for millennia have understood the relation between self-knowledge and the possibility of flourishing. Aristotle (384-322 BCE) claimed that the beginning of all wisdom is knowing yourself. Writing nearly 1800 years later, Montaigne (1533-1592 CE) extolled the virtue of being an expert on himself rather than being an expert on any other topic. He counsels us that

He who remembers the evils he has undergone, and those that have threatened him, and the slights causes that have changed him from one state to another, prepares himself in that way for future changes and for recognizing his condition. The life of Caesar has no more to show us than our own.…Let us only listen: we tell ourselves all we most need.

For Montaigne, we truly need to know what we are up against in our own selves, because all of that is a consequence of our experiences and the meaning we have given them. Coming to know when we feel resentment is as important as knowing what makes us feel gratitude. Knowing what sort of circumstance lend themselves to nerves or anxiety will help us to meet challenges in both the present and the future. Our past and our experiences have so much to teach us when we listen to ourselves.

article continues after advertisement

We need to look at the reflections of those fun house mirrors and understand them for the distortions that are. When we can do this, Montaigne might say, we are much more likely to belong to ourselves. When we do this, we can flourish.

item.title: Ambience Is a Key to the Perfect Shopping Experience
item.description:
Consumer Behavior

Ambience Is a Key to the Perfect Shopping Experience

Store ambience has the capacity to alter consumer behaviour.

Posted September 9, 2026

Key points
  • Creating ambience may not be easy.
  • But if you get it right it is possible to create positive perceptions through sensory input.
  • Increasingly, younger audiences have a preference for shops with ambience.

A recent survey of over 2000 people in three European countries found that creating the ‘right’ shopping environment can change how people behave whilst in-store and how much they spend. And it appears that some of the factors affecting our behaviours are clearly linked to our sensory systems, guiding our perception.

COVID-19 saw many consumers turn to independent shops, and many shoppers still prefer them to big brand shops. In fact, 75 percent of those surveyed in France, 80 percent in Britain, and 86 percent in Germany said that independent shops beat big chains on ambience. Apparently size matters.

The recent survey found that younger generations are particularly drawn to shops with ambience. Presumably, as it often generates pleasure and arousal. As many as 73-90 percent of surveyed Gen Zs said that they have avoided shops because it looked unwelcoming. This is presumably linked to a preference for experiential shopping, and ambience can be an important part. However, it is easy enough to say that a shop requires good ambience, but what constitutes a good shop atmosphere?

Environmental aspects, such as lighting and music, can create ambience and, in turn, influence consumers' emotional states and affect the likelihood of purchase. Moreover, ambience and the emotions it generates bring positive quality inferences for the shop itself, what is being sold, and the store image. Hence, if the ambience is right, most people will form an opinion of the shop within seconds of walking in; the consumer may not even be aware they have made up their mind about whether they like the shop.

Source: Courtesy of Youssef Quaatar on Pexels

Sensory input that contributes to good ambience

Scent, touch, wall colour, light, layout and music are examples of sensory input known to contribute to ambience. Sensory elements tend to work best when they are congruent with the products sold, as it then tends to produce more favourable evaluations.

Scent, for example, has been found to influence consumer decision-making depending on whether it is congruent with products. Pleasant fragrances can also put unknown brands in a better light and make consumers look at the products for longer.

Letting consumers touch products can make them feel more at ease in the store, as preventing people from touching can make them feel slightly frustrated, especially if they have a high need for touch, which many do. Touching products can also trigger ‘psychological ownership,’ when you feel as if the product already belongs to you. This is known to increase willingness to pay more for products; thus, they are less likely to question the price.

Lighting is another example, as it can influence how consumers perceive the overall shop, merchandise, and store image. Brightness can bring feelings of pleasure, which affects shopping intention, and warm lighting can enhance perception of quality.

What most of these factors have in common is that they directly or indirectly contribute to people spending more time within a store, as a good ambience makes them feel comfortable. Whilst consumers might be less aware of individual sensory input that contributes to ambience, they are clearly aware that ambience is important to them when they shop. Thus, they are more likely to seek out stores that make them feel good.

item.title: Support or Rescue: What Does the Nervous System Need?
item.description:
Child Development

Support or Rescue: What Does the Nervous System Need?

Being neurodivergent doesn't mean your child can't learn to tolerate distress.

Posted September 9, 2026

Key points
  • Neurodivergence doesn't mean your child can't tolerate any distress and needs to be rescued from it.
  • A diagnosis is a starting point for determining what a child needs, not a verdict on what they're capable of.
  • The goal is to figure out what is supportive versus enabling for your unique child, regardless of diagnosis.

Whenever I share a story about a child learning to move through distress instead of being rescued from it, some version of the same comment shows up: “This kid must not be neurodivergent.”

The implication is that a diagnosis of neurodivergence equals an inability to tolerate distress and a need for the environment to eradicate that distress.

This is not what I see in practice.

I work with many kids who have a diagnosis—ADHD, autism, anxiety, sensory processing differences—and many of them can build tolerance for distress, too.

The question isn’t, “Does this child have a diagnosis?” It’s, “What is this child’s actual capacity, in this specific situation, right now?”

Those are two very different questions. Conflating them is leading a lot of parents, especially parents of neurodivergent and highly sensitive kids, to accommodate far more than their child actually needs, out of fear that their nervous system can’t handle it.

Not to mention that diagnosis isn’t the whole story. For a lot of these kids, the diagnosis isn’t a bright line—it’s often, in part, a judgment call. While neurodevelopmental assessments include many standardized evaluation tools, clinical judgment leaves room for two experienced professionals to see the same child and land in different places. I’ve seen two kids with nearly identical patterns—similar epic meltdowns, similar drive for control, similar need for routine, similar rigidity—walk away with different labels. One child is ADHD, another ASD 1, another has anxiety, and another receives no diagnosis but is described as highly sensitive.

Don’t get me wrong. I’m not saying diagnoses are meaningless—they’re a starting point for figuring out what a child needs, not a verdict on what they’re capable of. A diagnosis doesn’t dictate whether to hold a limit or remove it.

Which leads me to my next point:

Regardless of diagnosis, children are not a monolithic group. While they may all have highly sensitive, reactive nervous systems—we know that their meltdowns aren’t manipulation, and that they can’t “just push through it”—the capacity for their systems to tolerate discomfort varies from child to child.

It’s all about figuring out what is supportive versus what is enabling for your unique child.

Support equals holding a limit that stretches a child a little past their current capacity, so they build the skill of coming back from dysregulation.

Enabling equals removing the challenge altogether, because you fear your child can’t work through the distress—it feels like too much.

article continues after advertisement

A diagnosis may mean a child needs more scaffolding, smaller steps, different kinds of support. It does not automatically mean a child can’t grow in a given area.

Milo, a 7-year-old with ASD 1, wants to be naked at home. His parents are sensitive to and fine with it, except when guests come over. They feel stuck; they love that Milo enjoys company but worry that setting this limit will overwhelm him and that he can’t do it.

Then they decide not to presuppose, to try setting a limit. They explain to Milo that when guests come over, the rule is that people need to be wearing something on top and bottom. He can choose any clothing that meets that criterion. If he wants to be naked, he can always be unclothed in his room and play there. This wasn’t punishment or even a natural consequence, just a limit. While Milo didn’t like it, they held firm. Milo ultimately adapted. He started choosing clothes on his own so he could be with the group.

5-year-old Lucy (no diagnosis; a very big reactor) has very low frustration tolerance. Every need is urgent: help getting her dress-up outfit on, carrying a heavy toy to another space, replacing the banana that broke. Her mom, Morgan, is very triggered by Lucy’s major meltdowns. She worries that Lucy’s nervous system can’t handle the distress. So she finds herself putting the baby down mid-feeding, getting off an important call, etc., to meet Lucy’s demands, which are only getting more fierce and frequent. This is making Morgan feel resentful towards Lucy for controlling her and the whole family.

When we meet, we come up with a plan that involves being sensitive to Lucy’s stress response without treating distress as an emergency.

It goes like this: “You really want my help right now. It’s hard to wait, I know. I’ll help you when I’m done feeding the baby.”

Then Morgan goes about feeding the baby and tolerates Lucy’s distress. In just a few weeks of taking this approach in similar situations, Lucy has become less demanding, more flexible, and, notably, seems happier and more content overall.

I hear this often from parents. It’s a relief to kids when their parents calmly hold a limit. Badgering, pushing their agenda, and throwing themselves on the floor in protest is exhausting.

I know you may have a lot of “yes buts”—that this would never work for your child. And you may be right.

These are not prescriptions. They’re examples of how doing the detective work to figure out what your child can handle, how they might level up with support, can work.

article continues after advertisement

The take-home: If you’re parenting a neurodivergent or highly sensitive child and you’ve been made to feel like holding any given limit is emotionally unsafe and harmful to them, that’s not universally true. You deserve support figuring out where your child’s actual edge is, not a blanket rule in either direction.
